title: The Fog Ferry's Secret
markdown:
The mist rolled in thick and wrapped Orin’s heart, cold and clammy. Fog. He hated it. It twisted the familiar river into a place for lurking shadows. Tonight was the worst — like trying to see through milk. The River Sprite groaned. A crack. Water rushed in, fast.

“It’s no good, Maela.” His voice was a whisper against the sighing wind. Knuckles white on the ferry’s edge. “We’ll sink before Elderwood Island.” Ankle-deep and rising.

Maela, perched like a sleek water bird, grinned that wide confident grin that always left him a little out of his depth. “Not if I can help it.” Dark hair glistened. Eyes sharp. Midnight swimmer. Fearless. She would dive into the darkest water and laugh the shadows off.

Elderwood needed medicine. Urgently. Old Man Hemlock, their healer, raged with fever. The supply boat was a week away. This damaged ferry, this foggy night: their only chance. Sunrise was the deadline. No medicine before dawn, and it might be too late.

“The fog—” Orin’s throat tightened. “I can’t see. The river is swallowing us.”

Maela slid off in a fluid motion, into the dark swirl, gone before he could protest. A thick rope around her waist; the other end on a post. Her anchor.

“I can feel the currents down here.” Muffled by mist. “I’ll guide you. Keep us moving. Steadily. Don’t let the fog get to you.”

The ferry was heavy, waterlogged, lurching. Water sloshed toward their knees. Orin’s hands trembled on the rudder. Shadows stretched and morphed in the grey. Maela’s pull and calm calls kept him from coming apart.

“Left a bit. Undertow. Hold steady. Submerged log. Steer clear.” She was the river’s whisper. Its secret language.

The rope went taut. The ferry lurched. Orin slammed the railing. “Maela!”

“Anchor snagged. I can’t free it. Current’s pulling us toward the rapids.”

Rapids. He had only seen them from afar: roar, white water, ruin. The ferry sank lower. Fog pressed, suffocating. He shut his eyes. Panic. Drowning before the boat did.

“Orin. The oars. Get us moving. I’ll swim around. Dislodge it from the other side.”

He forced his eyes open. The rapids’ hungry roar was constant. Maela was a dark silhouette plunging into the churn. A spark against the grey.

He was not only an apprentice. He was the ferryman. The responsibility felt solid. He grabbed the oars. Muscles screamed. He dug and pulled. He ignored the fog, the icy spray. He focused on current and on her struggle. Not fear this time — a fierce protective anger. For Maela. For the islanders. For the chance to be more than the boy who hated milk-thick nights.

He steered with a precision he did not know he had. Hands found angles. Body moved with the ferry. He wove the battered hull through treacherous water, guided by instinct and her work. Part of the river. Not its victim.

A final jarring lurch. Calm. Through. He leaned on the oars, gasping.

“We made it,” he whispered.

Maela hauled herself aboard, sputtering, triumphant, hair plastered, clothes heavy. She coughed, then beamed. “Told you. A little push.”

The sky blushed pink. Elderwood loomed through thinning mist. They tied up. Villagers rushed. Worry turned. Hemlock was weak, breathing shallow, eyes grateful as they put the medicine in his hands. A quiet warmth spread in Orin, more potent than fear. The fog was only a veil lifting.

He looked at Maela, mud-smudged, spirit undimmed. She offered a small knowing smile.

“You weren’t so afraid of the fog in the end.”

Orin’s smile reached his eyes. “I think I needed to see how brave I could be.”

The ember in his chest stayed. He was Orin, the ferryman. The river would fog again. He would still have oars, and a rope, and someone in the water who knew its language.
characters: Orin (an apprentice ferryman), Maela (a midnight swimmer)
